diagrams.title: Choose a multimodal task
diagrams.subtitle: The input, desired output and evaluation determine the route
trace: A help-desk chart plus 'Which day had the most tickets?' routes to the VLM.
A lighthouse description routes to the text-to-image pipeline instead.
A sentence routes to TTS; Whisper converts its generated waveform back to words.
Check each output with its own metric, then inspect metadata on the generated image.
diagrams.explanation: Multimodal generation covers several different tasks, so one score cannot evaluate every output. The input and desired output define the route. A vision-language model reads an image together with a question and generates answer text. A diffusion pipeline converts a description, or an image plus an editing request, into a new image. Text-to-speech converts a sentence into an audio waveform. Each route uses preprocessing suited to that model. Evaluation then asks a specific question: does the answer match a known chart value, does the image align with its prompt, or can speech recognition recover the words? These checks cover only part of quality. Finally, the lab adds metadata to a generated image and resaves it as JPEG, demonstrating that a provenance label can disappear during ordinary file processing.
diagrams.check_question: Can a good CLIP score demonstrate that generated speech sounds natural?
diagrams.check_answer: No. This lab's CLIP score measures image-text alignment; speech naturalness needs a speech-appropriate evaluation.

diagrams.insert_before_title: Real captions from an open VLM
diagrams.title: From picture and question to words
diagrams.subtitle: A vision-language model connects visual features to text generation
diagrams.feedback: New tokens extend the answer prefix for the next prediction.
trace: Pass the help-desk chart and 'How many tickets were there on Thursday?' to ask.
The processor prepares the chart and formats the question as model inputs.
Visual features provide evidence; the decoder generates an answer token by token.
ask decodes only the new answer tokens, leaving the input prompt out.
Compare the answer with the known value 25; a fluent answer may still be wrong.
diagrams.explanation: A vision-language model, or VLM, combines visual understanding with language generation. The lab's processor prepares the image and formats a chat message containing the question. Inside the selected model, a vision component encodes pixels into features; a connection to the language component makes those features usable alongside question tokens. The precise bridge depends on the model architecture, while the lab calls the same high-level generation interface. Generation is autoregressive: every new token is predicted using the input and the answer prefix generated so far. A decoder then converts token IDs into readable words. The ask function slices away the input token prefix before decoding the output. The model can produce confident text even when it misreads a chart, so the known chart values provide evidence for checking rather than trusting fluency.
diagrams.check_question: Why does ask remove the input token prefix before decoding?
diagrams.check_answer: To return the newly generated answer rather than repeat the question and chat prompt.

diagrams.title: Generate, inspect and evaluate
diagrams.subtitle: Follow three model routes and a provenance experiment
trace: Inspect the chart values and fictional invoice fields before calling the VLM.
Compare model answers with known answers and inspect any incorrect result.
Generate the lighthouse image; compare the original with edits at three strengths.
Compare original sentences with Whisper's recovered text, then listen to the audio.
Print the PNG metadata and compare it with the resaved JPEG's metadata.
diagrams.explanation: This lab contains several experiments rather than one model that performs every task. The first route uses ask for captions, chart questions and a fictional invoice. The score helper is a small heuristic: it checks a text substring or the first parsed number, so inspect full answers as well as its score. A separate diffusion route generates images and performs editing at different strengths. The clip_score function checks whether generated images align with their prompts, without establishing factual accuracy or complete visual quality. The speech route synthesises a waveform, transcribes it with Whisper and compares words using WER. That round trip measures recoverability through one recogniser, rather than human listening quality. The final PNG-to-JPEG experiment inspects how an attached AI-generation label can be lost after resharing.
diagrams.check_question: If WER is zero in the speech round trip, what has been demonstrated?
diagrams.check_answer: Whisper recovered the reference words after normalisation. Naturalness, emotion and human listening quality still require separate checks.

diagrams.title: Teach a visual bridge and useful answers
diagrams.subtitle: A conceptual training recipe; this lab loads existing models
diagrams.insert_before_title: A typical training pipeline for a vision-language model
diagrams.explanation: A modular vision-language model can start from an existing image encoder and language model. The image encoder produces visual features, but those features are not automatically in the form the language model expects. A learned bridge, often called a projector, maps them into suitable vectors. An alignment stage uses image-caption examples to train that connection. Visual instruction tuning then uses questions and desired answers about images, documents or charts. Different recipes train different components; some keep the image encoder fixed and add LoRA to the language model. Held-out images check whether the system generalises beyond its examples. This is a conceptual recipe: the lab loads pretrained models and measures inference, rather than training a VLM.
trace: An image of a cup is paired with "a blue cup on a desk".
The bridge learns to present the visual features to the language model.
An instruction example asks "What colour is the cup?" with answer "blue".
A new cup photo tests reading accuracy without appearing in training.
diagrams.check_question: Does the multimodal lab train the illustrated bridge?
diagrams.check_answer: No. It loads existing models; the diagram explains how such a model can be built.

diagrams.title: Read an invoice and verify the numbers
diagrams.subtitle: Separate visual extraction from arithmetic and factual checking
diagrams.insert_before_title: Cross-modal reasoning over a chart and a document (real)
diagrams.explanation: The invoice example distinguishes seeing a number from calculating with it. The lab creates a fictional invoice from known strings and values, so there is a reference to check. The ask function supplies the image and question to a vision-language model, which returns a candidate answer. The score function gives a small automatic check, but its substring or first-number rule can miss some errors. Read the full reply alongside the source. For a real invoice application, extract fields into a validated structure and sum them in ordinary code; compare that result with the printed total. The final block describes that application design, rather than a complete invoice-processing service supplied by the notebook.
trace: Suppose visible lines show EUR 10 and EUR 20, with printed total EUR 30.
Ask for each amount separately before computing the total.
If one extracted amount is EUR 200, valid numeric format still hides a reading error.
Code computes 10 + 20 = 30; review a mismatch with the image.
diagrams.check_question: Can a correct addition still produce a wrong invoice total?
diagrams.check_answer: Yes. Code can add incorrectly extracted numbers perfectly; check the input values too.

glossary.meaning: A vision-language model that uses images and text together.
A learned mapping connecting feature dimensions or representation spaces.
An output claim that is unsupported by the supplied input or evidence.
Generation through learned denoising of a noisy representation.
An image-to-image setting controlling how much the input is perturbed before denoising.
Text-to-speech: turning written words into an audio waveform.
Automatic speech recognition: turning speech audio into text.
Information about a media item's origin and editing history.

pitfalls: A fluent description can mention objects absent from the image; compare claims with visible evidence.
A strong image-text alignment score or a low speech WER covers only one aspect of output quality.
A PNG text label can be removed or forged; it does not prove an unbroken origin history.

recap.example: Invoice image → extracted fields → checked amounts → code sum → review any mismatch.
recap.question: Code sums extracted amounts correctly. Can the final total still be wrong?
recap.answer: Yes. An extracted amount may have been misread; check values against the image as well.
recap.next: In Week 11 we package models into monitored applications.
recap.notes: Return to the receipt from the warm-up. Ask students to separate reading a value from calculating with it. Reconstruct the VLM path from pixels and question to new answer tokens. Name the bridge as a learned mapping, then distinguish conceptual training from the frozen models used in the lab. Compare the image and speech routes: they create different outputs and require different measures. A CLIP score checks alignment; speech WER checks recovered words through one recogniser. Neither covers all quality. End by explaining why a removable PNG label is not signed provenance and why a correct sum can still use wrongly extracted values.
